```{r setup}
library(seir)
```

We follow the general approach in Wu et al (2020) to fit a model of transmission dynamics in Wuhan to exported case incidence, but using particle Markov chain Monte Carlo to account for stochastic transmission, rather than the deterministic MCMC fitting used in the original paper. We use a basic SIR model, here specified as a pre-compiled [`odin` model](https://mrc-ide.github.io/odin/) called `sir` generated from the odin code defined in `inst/odin/sir.R`.

First, we load international onset data from the repository accompanying the Kucharski et al (2020) early analysis of Wuhan dynamics, and format accordingly:
```{r}
# Load Wuhan data
international_onset_data_in <- read.csv("~/Documents/GitHub/2020-ncov/stoch_model/data/time_series_WHO_report.csv")
international_onset_data_in$date <- as.Date(international_onset_data_in$date)

incidence <- international_onset_data_in$number

n_steps <- length(incidence)
dt <- 1

# Convert to required format
data_raw <- data.frame(day = seq(1,n_steps*dt),cases = incidence)
data <- mcstate::particle_filter_data(data_raw,"day",1/dt)

plot(data_raw$day,data_raw$cases,type = "l",xlab = "Day",ylab = "Cases")
```
We then define a function to allow us to compare a model output (`state`) with observed data (`observed`) using a Poisson observation model. We scale model predicted cases based on the probability of a given Wuhan resident travelling internationally (i.e. 3633 daily outbound travellers divided by a population of 19 million).
```{r}
# Define comparison function
# Travel data
prob <- 3633/19e6

compare <- function(state, observed, pars = NULL) {
  exp_noise <- 1e6

  incidence_modelled <- state[5, , drop = TRUE]
  incidence_observed <- observed$cases
  lambda <- incidence_modelled*prob 
  dpois(x = incidence_observed, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE)
}
```
Next, we define the particle filter that propagates a set of particles of size `n_particles` over time, with each particle representing a single output from the model (`seirdage`). At each time step, the particle filter uses the comparison function (`compare`) and observed data (`data`) to weight and resample the particles.

We assume a fully susceptible population initially, and 10 infectious individuals on the first day of the analysis (i.e. 30th Dec 2019).

**Note: need to check inputs are defined properly in the model/particle filter object here**
```{r}
# Define initial conditions
dt <- 1
S_ini <- 19e6
I_ini <- 1

# Create particle filter
filter <- mcstate::particle_filter$new(data = data,
                              model = sir,
                              n_particles = 100,
                              compare = compare,
                              seed = 1)

filter$run(save_history = TRUE, pars = list(dt = dt,S_ini = S_ini,I_ini = I_ini))
#S_ini = S_ini,I_ini = I_ini,beta = 0.03,sigma = 0.5,gamma = 0.1))

plot_particle_filter <- function(history, true_history, times, obs_end = NULL) {
    if (is.null(obs_end)) {
        obs_end = max(times)
    }
    
    par(mar = c(4.1, 5.1, 0.5, 0.5), las = 1)
    cols <- c(I = "#cc0044") #, R = "#999966") #S = "#8c8cd9", 
    matplot(times, t(history[3, , -1]), type = "l",
            xlab = "Time", ylab = "Number of individuals",
            col = scales::alpha(cols[["I"]],0.1), lty = 1, ylim = range(history[3, , -1]))
    #matlines(times, t(history[3, , -1]), col = scales::alpha(cols[["I"]],0.1), lty = 1)
    #matlines(times, t(history[4, , -1]), col = scales::alpha(cols[["R"]],0.1), lty = 1)
    # matpoints(times[1:obs_end], t(true_history[1:3, , -1]), pch = 19,
    #           col = cols)
    legend("left", lwd = 1, col = cols, legend = names(cols), bty = "n")
}

plot_particle_filter(filter$history(), true_history, data_raw$day)
```
With the model, data, and particle filter defined, we use particle MCMC (pMCMC) to estimate the posterior parameters of the model, given the observed data and a set of priors. We transform parameters into a compatible input object and define a proposal matrix for the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference, then run pMCMC:
```{r}
# Set up MCMC
R0 <- mcstate::pmcmc_parameter("R0", 2, min = 0)
gamma <- mcstate::pmcmc_parameter("gamma", 0.1, min = 0,
                         prior = function(p)
                             dgamma(p, shape = 1, scale = 0.2, log = TRUE))

make_transform <- function(pars,dt,S_ini,I_ini){
    function(pars){
        beta <- pars[["R0"]] * pars[["gamma"]]
        gamma <- pars[["gamma"]]
        list(beta = beta,gamma = gamma,dt = dt,S_ini = S_ini,I_ini = I_ini)
    }
}

transform <- make_transform(pars,dt,S_ini,I_ini)

proposal_matrix <- matrix(c(0.01^2, 0, 0, 0.01^2), nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
mcmc_pars <- mcstate::pmcmc_parameters$new(list(R0 = R0, gamma = gamma), proposal_matrix, transform = transform)

# Run pMCMC
control <- mcstate::pmcmc_control(
    500,
    save_state = TRUE,
    save_trajectories = TRUE,
    progress = TRUE)
pmcmc_run <- mcstate::pmcmc(mcmc_pars, filter, control = control)
```
We then plot the estimated infection dynamics:
```{r}
# Plot fitted trajectories
plot_particle_filter(pmcmc_run$trajectories$state, true_history, data_raw$day)
```
And summarise the parameter estimates
```{r}
# Summarise and plot MCMC output
# processed_chains <- pmcmc_thin(pmcmc_run, burnin = 200, thin = 2)
# parameter_mean_hpd <- apply(processed_chains$pars, 2, mean)
# parameter_mean_hpd
mcmc1 <- coda::as.mcmc(cbind(pmcmc_run$probabilities, pmcmc_run$pars))
summary(mcmc1)
```
Finally, we estimate the number of infections as of 26th Jan 2020:

```{r}
output_infections <- pmcmc_run$trajectories$state[3,,length(data_raw$day)]
quantile(output_infections,c(0.025,0.5,0.975))
```
